text: former coworkers. “Next time you decide to die mid-trial and not tell anyone, I’m sedating you with a tranq dart and dragging your ass back by your ankles.” To one side, Dwight full-on snorted. David groaned into his hands, wishing he could be anywhere else. This constant piercing attention was wearing him down. Though the sarcasm and over the top empty threats were a nice relief from the weight of the earlier tension. And just like that, the air lightened. The tension didn’t vanish, but it shifted. Relented. Turned into something livable. The wound still ached. But it felt like it could start to heal now. The fire had settled into a low, steady crackle. Jill leaned back against the log with the smug look of a woman who knew exactly how to break up a fistfight without lifting a finger. Dwight had taken up poking half-heartedly at the flames with a twig, still trying to process everything, a light grin ghosting across his expression. And David... David just sat there. Shoulders low. Head bowed. One arm curled tight against his ribs, the bruising hidden under his shirt. Felix shifted in place — his posture opening up, less tense now, though his brows still hadn’t fully smoothed. “You really scared me,” No bite. No edge. Disappointed irritation finally worn down to something softer. David nodded once. “Yeah... I didn’t mean to.” “I know.” Felix exhaled like he’d been holding it all night. “I thought you trusted me.” David’s hand curled a little tighter over his ribs. “I do,” he murmured. “I just... I’m not used to being the one who needs watching.” Felix hummed — somewhere between a sigh and a tired laugh. “Yeah, well. Maybe get used to it.” David looked over at that — finally meeting Felix’s eyes. The pride and bravado he wore like armor softened into something quieter. Gratitude. “...You did good,” he murmured. “Back there. Getting me out.” Felix shrugged, looking away before the moment could settle too deep. “Didn’t feel like dragging your corpse back to camp, that’s all.” He nudged a twig with his boot. “You’re heavy.” David huffed, the edge of a laugh pulling at his bruised ribs. “Wow. Thanks for the concern.” “Anytime.” They sat like that for a while — a tired calm, no longer on edge. A peace truce forged from bruises and barely avoided catastrophe. The fire popped. The night moved on. And maybe — just maybe — the bond between them had settled into something a little more solid.
